title: Education Reform Needs More “Go Energy”
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman responds to Michael Petrilli's call for state education agencies to "just do things" by arguing that the energy would be better channelled through individuals than through big state policy. Having been burned by large policy efforts, he would rather government leaders clear barriers, create incentives, and let others try new things. He says K-12 has too much "stop energy" and too little "go energy," and that the right has found its energy in school choice while the left has not. His quick list for progressive reformers includes starting charters and microschools, organizing parents for magnet seats and open enrollment, helping parents navigate choice, building public scholarship-granting organizations, teaching kids to read early, expanding math acceleration, and building more routes through high school. A short section cites new research showing widening inequality in parental spending on child development, and a reading list closes the post.
points: Aldeman prefers individual and community action to sweeping state mandates, and asks government to clear barriers and give others room to try.
His diagnosis is that K-12 has too much stop energy, and that the political left lacks the energy the right has shown for school choice.
He lists seven concrete actions, from starting teacher-led schools to expanding dual enrollment and career pathways.
He cites research that the gap in spending on child development between the top 10 percent and bottom 25 percent grew from roughly 3 times to more than 13 times between 1980 and 2024.
The post concedes that not every effort will work but insists that waiting for permission guarantees nothing is found.
quotes: In my view, K-12 education has been riddled with too much “stop energy” and not enough “go energy,” in the words of Jennifer Pahlka.
If government leaders are tired of watching student achievement slide in their communities, I’d rather they clear barriers, create incentives, and give other people room to try stuff.
Start new charter schools, microschools, or other teacher-led programs—or help successful ones grow.
Organize parents to push for more seats in popular magnet schools and better open enrollment policies.
Not every effort will work. But we won’t find the ones that do by waiting for permission.
By 2024, that difference had grown to more than $7,000 per child, with the top 10 percent spending more than 13 times as much as the bottom 25 percent
